summary: Al-Andalus is the Arabic name for the parts of the Iberian peninsula under Muslim rule from the conquest of 711 to the fall of Nasrid Granada in 1492, a territory that shrank over the centuries and passed through an Umayyad emirate (756) and caliphate (929), the taifa kingdoms, Almoravid and Almohad rule, and the Nasrid emirate. It names both a polity and an Arabic-Islamic civilization, in which the Maliki school of law predominated and Muslim, Jewish, and Christian scholars produced a large body of law, theology, philosophy, mysticism, and poetry, and it became an enduring object of memory and nostalgia in Arabic and Hebrew literature.
description: Al-Andalus came into being with the Umayyad conquest of 711 and was governed at first by governors who, as al-Maqqari records, were appointed either by the governors of Africa or by the Umayyad caliphs and bore no title but amir. After the Abbasid Revolution of 750, the Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman I, who had escaped the killing of his family, defeated the last governor, Yusuf al-Fihri, and entered Cordoba on the feast of the sacrifice, 10 Dhu al-Hijja 138 (May 756), as al-Maqqari dates it, founding an independent emirate. Al-Maqqari also records that Abd al-Aziz, the first governor after the conquest, held his court at Seville and that his successor Ayyub ibn Habib moved the seat of government to Cordoba. In 316/929 Abd al-Rahman III took the title of caliph (amir al-mu'minin) with the regnal name al-Nasir li-din Allah; Maribel Fierro reads the claim against the rival Fatimid caliphate in North Africa and the Abbasids in Baghdad, and the Cordoban caliphate marked the height of Umayyad power in the west. After a civil war (fitna) from 399/1009 the caliphate was abolished in 422/1031, and al-Andalus divided into competing taifa ('party') kingdoms, which were drawn into tribute and war with the expanding Christian kingdoms of the north; the fall of Toledo to Castile in 478/1085 led the taifa rulers to call in the Almoravids (al-Murabitun), a Berber movement from the Maghrib, who ruled al-Andalus from the late eleventh century, and they were followed from the mid-twelfth century by the Almohads (al-Muwahhidun), whose movement claimed reform of doctrine in the name of the unity of God. After the Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa (609/1212) and the Castilian conquest (from the Muslim side, the fall) of Cordoba (1236) and Seville (1248), stages of what later Spanish historiography called the 'Reconquista', a term whose use is itself debated (Ríos Saloma), only the Nasrid emirate of Granada remained, until its surrender to the Catholic Monarchs in 897/1492. Religious life was shaped by the dominance of the Maliki school of law, which Hugh Kennedy and Maribel Fierro describe as closely tied to the Umayyad state and its judges; dissenting currents existed, most visibly Ibn Hazm of Cordoba (d. 456/1064), the Zahiri jurist and theologian, who held that the law is to be derived from the apparent (zahir) sense of the Qur'an and Sunna, and whose polemics against the Maliki jurists and other schools made him a controversial figure whose books were publicly burned. The intellectual world of al-Andalus included the philosopher, Maliki judge, and Aristotle commentator Ibn Rushd (Averroes, d. 1198), who served the Almohads; the Sufi metaphysician Ibn Arabi (d. 1240), born in Murcia; and Jewish scholars writing in Arabic, Judeo-Arabic, and Hebrew, among them the poet and author of the Kuzari Judah Halevi, the exegete and poet Abraham ibn Ezra, and Maimonides, born in Cordoba, whose family left al-Andalus after the Almohad conquest. Jews and Christians lived under Muslim rule as protected communities (ahl al-dhimma). Christians under Muslim rule are conventionally, though contestedly, called Mozarabs; their own Latin writings, among them the Chronicle of 754 and the accounts of the Cordoban martyrs of the 850s, are the subject of Ann Christys's study of the Christians of al-Andalus in their own words. A Jewish voice is the Sefer ha-Qabbalah (c. 1161) of Abraham ibn Daud of Toledo, which narrates the transmission of rabbinic learning to al-Andalus and the leadership of Jewish courtiers under its Muslim rulers. How the situation of both communities should be characterized is debated by modern historians under the heading of convivencia. After 1492 al-Andalus became an object of memory: elegies for lost cities were composed while the Christian conquest advanced, and Alexander Elinson studies how Andalusi Arabic and Hebrew writers made al-Andalus a literary image of loss and nostalgia; in the seventeenth century the Maghribi scholar al-Maqqari, writing in Cairo, compiled the Nafh al-tib, a vast anthology of the history and literature of al-Andalus. Modern scholarship differs over how to characterize the polity: Eduardo Manzano Moreno questions both the image of a tribal society and idealized pictures of al-Andalus, and Salma Khadra Jayyusi's The Legacy of Muslim Spain, which brings Arab and European scholars together, opens with the Egyptian historian Mahmoud Makki's political history of al-Andalus from 92/711 to 897/1492.
editorial_notes: This concept names Muslim-ruled Iberia as a polity and a civilization, not a single datable happening; the datable boundaries are held by the event entries for the conquest of 711 and the fall of Granada in 1492, to which it links. It is filed under islam per ADR-0010 because it names a Muslim polity; the home is a storage convention, not a claim of ownership, and the history of al-Andalus is equally part of Jewish and Christian history, linked through relations (convivencia, sephardic-diaspora, expulsion-from-spain, moriscos) and the Jewish figures of its intellectual world. NEUTRALITY: no characterization of al-Andalus as a 'golden age' of tolerance or as a regime of oppression is adopted; that question is described as a historiographical debate, and the entry links to convivencia (principles #1 and #2). The Christian conquests are named in both registers (Castilian conquest; from the Muslim side, the fall), and 'Reconquista' is named as a contested term attributed to Ríos Saloma. Ibn Hazm's Zahiri method is described in its own terms, and the name 'Mozarabs' is flagged as conventional and contested. The Almohad movement is described by its own claim to doctrinal reform, and Ibn Hazm's controversy is described as such, without ruling on the disputes. The status of Jews and Christians as protected communities is stated as the legal category, not evaluated. Andalusian nostalgia is described as a literary tradition studied by Elinson, not as a judgment on the past. SOURCING (principles #8 and #9): (a) modern academic historians, Kennedy (1996), Fierro (2005), Manzano Moreno (2006), Adang, Fierro, and Schmidtke (eds., 2013) on Ibn Hazm, and Elinson (2009) on literary memory; (b) the classical Arabic tradition's own compendium of Andalusi history and literature, al-Maqqari's Nafh al-tib in Gayangos's partial translation, read directly for the governors and the accession of Abd al-Rahman I; (c) an Arab and Muslim scholar writing academically, the Egyptian historian Mahmoud Makki's political history of al-Andalus in Jayyusi (ed., 1992). The Christian voice under Muslim rule is represented through Christys (2002), and a Jewish voice through Abraham ibn Daud's Sefer ha-Qabbalah in Gerson D. Cohen's edition and translation (1967). Ríos Saloma's introduction (pp. 30-32, UNAM open edition) was read directly and is rated high. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited; the two Brill Handbook of Oriental Studies volumes cited are scholarly edited monographs with signed chapters, not reference works. Al-Maqqari in Gayangos's translation was read directly in the public-domain scan for the governors of al-Andalus, Abd al-Aziz's court at Seville and the transfer to Cordoba, and Abd al-Rahman I's entry into Cordoba on 10 Dhu al-Hijja 138 (vol. 2, Book V, ch. 5, pp. 55-56; the translation misprints the CE year of that entry as 750, and the hijri date is followed here), so it is rated high for those claims. The page range of Makki's chapter could not be verified and is not given. The other sources, apart from Ríos Saloma as noted above, were verified to exist and to be on-topic through publisher pages, library catalogues, and reviews but were not read line by line, so they are rated medium. Dates are given in hijri and CE where the sources conventionally give both.

historical_period.note: From the Umayyad conquest of 711 to the surrender of Nasrid Granada in January 1492. The territory of al-Andalus shrank over the period, and Muslim communities (Mudejars, later Moriscos) remained under Christian rule after the end of Muslim political power, until the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609-1614.

relations.note: The conquest of 711 began Muslim rule in the peninsula and the history of al-Andalus.
The surrender of the Nasrid emirate of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492 ended Muslim political rule in Iberia and closes the history of al-Andalus as a polity.
Al-Andalus was first a province of the Umayyad caliphate of Damascus; Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed a caliphate at Cordoba in 929, which lasted until 1031.
The Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman I, a survivor of the Abbasid Revolution of 750, founded the independent emirate of Cordoba in 756.
The legal school named after Malik ibn Anas predominated in al-Andalus and was closely associated with its Umayyad rulers and judges.
Al-Andalus is a principal historical example of a region where one school of law, the Maliki, was predominant, alongside dissenting currents such as Ibn Hazm's Zahiri school.
Ibn Rushd (Averroes), philosopher, Maliki judge, and commentator on Aristotle, was born in Cordoba and served the Almohad rulers of al-Andalus and the Maghrib.
The Sufi metaphysician Ibn Arabi was born in Murcia in 1165 and formed in al-Andalus before settling in the east.
Al-Andalus was one of the centres of the Arabic philosophical tradition, above all through Ibn Rushd's Aristotle commentaries.
Maimonides was born in Cordoba; his family left al-Andalus after the Almohad conquest, and he composed his works in Judeo-Arabic and Hebrew in the Maghrib and Egypt.
Judah Halevi, poet and author of the Kuzari, lived in Muslim and Christian Spain and belongs to the Hebrew and Judeo-Arabic literary culture of al-Andalus.
Abraham ibn Ezra, exegete, grammarian, and poet, was born in Tudela and formed in the Hebrew literary culture of al-Andalus before leaving Spain around 1140.
Jews and Christians lived in al-Andalus as protected communities under Islamic law, a status grounded in their classification as People of the Book.
How the coexistence of Muslims, Christians, and Jews in al-Andalus should be characterized is one of the central questions of the modern historiographical debate over convivencia.
After the end of Muslim rule, the descendants of the Muslims of al-Andalus forcibly converted to Christianity in the early sixteenth century were known as Moriscos.
The Jews of Sefarad, many of whose communities had flourished under Muslim rule in al-Andalus, were dispersed after the expulsions of 1492 and 1497.

sources.citation: Kennedy, Hugh. Muslim Spain and Portugal: A Political History of al-Andalus. London and New York: Longman, 1996. Academic political history of al-Andalus from the conquest of 711 to the fall of Granada in 1492, including the emirate, caliphate, taifas, Almoravids, Almohads, and Nasrids, with discussion of the Arabic sources; the academic-history lens. Verified via library catalogues and reviews (Journal of Ecclesiastical History; Review of Middle East Studies). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary; cited for reference, relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Fierro, Maribel. Abd al-Rahman III: The First Cordoban Caliph. Makers of the Muslim World. Oxford: Oneworld, 2005. Academic biography of the first Umayyad ruler of al-Andalus to take the title of caliph (929), treating the caliphal claim, its rivals, and the Maliki religious establishment; the academic-history lens. Verified via the publisher and a review by Janina Safran in the International Journal of Middle East Studies. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary; cited for reference, relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Manzano Moreno, Eduardo. Conquistadores, emires y califas: los omeyas y la formación de al-Andalus. Barcelona: Crítica, 2006. Academic history of the formation of al-Andalus from the conquest to the end of the Umayyad caliphate, drawing on Arabic and Latin texts, archaeology, and numismatics, and questioning both the image of a tribal society and idealized pictures of al-Andalus; the academic-history lens. Verified via publisher records and a review in Estudios de Historia de España (2007). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Adang, Camilla, Maribel Fierro, and Sabine Schmidtke, eds. Ibn Hazm of Cordoba: The Life and Works of a Controversial Thinker. Handbook of Oriental Studies, Section 1, 103. Leiden and Boston: Brill, 2013. Scholarly edited volume on the Zahiri jurist, theologian, and man of letters Ibn Hazm (d. 456/1064), including his literalism, his polemics, the burning of his books, and his place in al-Andalus; the academic-history lens. Verified via the publisher and library records. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Makki, Mahmoud. 'The Political History of al-Andalus (92/711-897/1492).' In The Legacy of Muslim Spain, ed. Salma Khadra Jayyusi (with Manuela Marín, chief consultant). The opening chapter of the History section, a political history of al-Andalus from the conquest to the fall of Granada by an Egyptian historian of al-Andalus, in a volume that brings Arab and European scholars together; the modern Arab and Muslim scholarly lens. sources.citation: al-Maqqari, Ahmad ibn Muhammad. Nafh al-tib min ghusn al-Andalus al-ratib, partially translated as The History of the Mohammedan Dynasties in Spain, trans. Pascual de Gayangos. 2 vols. London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1840-1843. Vol. 2, Book V, ch. 5 (chapter opens p. 40), pp. 55-56: the chronology of the governors of al-Andalus compiled by al-Maqqari (d. 1041/1632), including their appointment by the governors of Africa or the Umayyad caliphs with the title amir only, Abd al-Aziz's court at Seville, Ayyub ibn Habib's transfer of the seat of government to Cordoba, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya's defeat of the governor Yusuf and entry into Cordoba on 10 Dhu al-Hijja 138. The Muslim primary-text lens and itself a monument of later Andalusian memory; the passages used were read directly in the public-domain scan.
sources.license: Public domain (1843 translation; underlying Arabic text public domain). Read directly for the passages cited.

sources.citation: Elinson, Alexander E. Looking Back at al-Andalus: The Poetics of Loss and Nostalgia in Medieval Arabic and Hebrew Literature. Brill Studies in Middle Eastern Literatures 34. Leiden and Boston: Brill, 2009. Study of Andalusi Arabic elegies for lost cities, prose, and the Hebrew qasida on al-Andalus and Sefarad, showing how these literatures made al-Andalus an image of loss and nostalgia; the academic lens on later memory. Verified via library catalogues (CiNii; ARCE). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary; cited for reference, relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Christys, Ann. Christians in al-Andalus, 711-1000. Culture and Civilization in the Middle East. Richmond: Curzon, 2002. Academic study reconsidering, through their own Latin writings (the chronicles on the fate of Hispania, the accounts of the Cordoban martyrs, and other texts), the history of the Christians of al-Andalus; the academic lens on the Christian voice under Muslim rule. Verified via library catalogues and reviews (Bulletin critique des Annales islamologiques; Collectanea Christiana Orientalia). Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Ibn Daud, Abraham. A Critical Edition with a Translation and Notes of the Book of Tradition (Sefer ha-Qabbalah), ed. and trans. Gerson D. Cohen. Judaica Texts and Translations 3. Hebrew chronicle (c. 1161) by a Jewish philosopher and historian of Toledo, defending the continuity of rabbinic tradition and narrating its transmission to al-Andalus; the primary-text lens (Jewish voice). sources.citation: Ríos Saloma, Martín F. La Reconquista: una construcción historiográfica (siglos XVI-XIX). Madrid: Marcial Pons Historia; México: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 2011. 352 pp. ISBN 978-84-92820-47-4. Academic study of how the term and idea of the Reconquista were constructed in Spanish historiography; its introduction distinguishes five senses of the term, including a period 'desde la batalla de Covadonga en 718 hasta la conquista de Granada en 1492' and 'una categoría historiográfica', and argues that 'el mito de la Reconquista se reinventó en el siglo xix'. The introduction (pp. 30-32) was read directly in the open-access UNAM digital edition (2016).
